---
title: What encryption does and doesn't do
description: Every video is stored and streamed as AES-128 encrypted HLS, which protects your storage but is not DRM.
icon: Lock
---

Every output ClipMux writes is encrypted. That keeps your stored videos
useless to anyone who gets at the bucket or the disk, and makes a leaked
segment URL worthless on its own. It does not stop a viewer who may watch a
video from saving it. This page says plainly where the line is.

## What it does

- **Every segment is encrypted with AES-128**, the standard HLS encryption
  that every HLS player supports. You turn nothing on.
- **Storage holds only ciphertext.** Segments, and subtitles and chapters
  files, are encrypted at rest. A leaked bucket, stolen storage credentials
  or a copied disk exposes no playable output.
- **The key is handed out behind the token.** Each media playlist names its
  key by a URL that carries the same token as the segments. Delivery answers
  only a request that passes the same checks: a `v` token for that playback
  ID, or a public playback ID. A `t` (poster-only) token can't fetch it, and
  the answer is never cached.
- **Keys are derived, not stored.** Each output's key is derived on request
  from the server's content key secret, the video's ID and the output's ID.
  There is no table of keys to leak, and a token for one video can't fetch
  another video's key.
- **Each output has its own key.** A re-encode brings a new key, so a leaked
  key exposes one version of one video.
- **The secret is sealed.** The content key secret is stored in Postgres,
  encrypted with a key held outside it. A worker that encodes a video
  receives only the key for the output it writes.

## What it doesn't do

- **It is not DRM.** Anyone with a valid token can fetch the key, and common
  download tools do that automatically. A viewer you let watch a video can
  save it, and anyone can record their screen. ClipMux has no Widevine,
  FairPlay or PlayReady, and no licence server.
- **It doesn't replace tokens.** Encryption is a layer behind access
  control. Who may watch is decided by your backend when it signs a token,
  and by revoking playback IDs. A public playback ID serves its key to
  anyone, by design.
- **It doesn't encrypt the source.** The file you upload is kept as
  uploaded, in the same storage, so it can be encoded again. Protect the
  bucket or disk as you would any copy of your videos. See
  [Where videos are stored](/docs/self-host/storage).

To limit what a leaked token can do, keep tokens short and pass a `vid`
claim, so analytics can show who watched. See
[Playback IDs and tokens](/docs/build/concepts/playback-ids-and-tokens).

## If the secret leaks

The server's owner rotates the content key secret, and re-encodes the
videos that matter. New outputs use the new secret; old outputs keep playing
with the version they were made with until they are encoded again. Losing
the secret, or the key that seals it, makes every output unplayable, so it
belongs in backups. See [Rotate keys and secrets](/docs/self-host/operate/rotate-secrets)
and [Back up and restore](/docs/self-host/operate/backups).
